paras.text: Essential Insurance Act and Market Audio Lecture

Welcome to the Essential Insurance Act chapter. This is the chapter that controls whether a Michigan insurer can turn you down for home insurance, whether it can drop you after a claim, and what it must tell you when it does either. It sits behind almost every nonrenewal letter a homeowner brings you. Chapter twenty one, M C L five hundred point twenty one zero one and following, carries three names on the statute text itself: Act two eighteen, Essential Insurance, and No Fault Insurance. Added in nineteen seventy nine, it covers both automobile and home insurance. We cover only the home half.

First trap. Twenty one zero one is not the purpose section. Open it and you find one sentence: the words and phrases defined in sections twenty one zero two to twenty one zero four have the meanings given in those sections. It is a pointer. Definitions live across three sections: twenty one zero two covers A to D, twenty one zero three E to I, twenty one zero four P to U. Learn that split, because the chapter's two biggest terms, eligible person and home insurance, both sit in twenty one zero three.

So who is an eligible person for home insurance? Under twenty one zero three, subsection two, the owner occupant or tenant of a house, condominium unit, cooperative unit, room, or apartment, or the owner occupant of a building of no more than four residential units. The statute then carves people OUT with a list worth knowing cold. It is the menu a carrier leans on. A conviction within the preceding five years for arson, conspiracy to commit arson, or one of the listed Michigan penal code burning and property destruction crimes knocks you out. So does a successful insurer denial of a home claim based on arson or fraud in that same five year window, or insuring a dwelling used for an illegal or demonstrably hazardous purpose. Refusing to buy enough insurance disqualifies, with three thresholds: at least eighty percent of replacement cost under a replacement cost policy, one hundred percent of market value under a repair cost policy, and one hundred percent of actual cash value under a tenant or renter's policy. A nonpayment cancellation within the preceding two years knocks you out, unless the premium is paid in full before the policy issues or renews. There are dollar floors on insured value: at least fifteen thousand dollars for a repair cost policy, at least thirty five thousand dollars, or another amount the director sets by rule, for a replacement policy. Rounding out the list: physical conditions presenting an extreme likelihood of a significant loss, property taxes delinquent two or more years at renewal, and failing to keep a uniformly required club or organization membership.

What does home insurance mean here? Fire insurance for a dwelling of the type just described, plus other nonbusiness coverage bundled into or endorsed onto that fire policy, plus whatever the director adds by rule. It excludes anything meant to insure commercial, industrial, professional, or business property, obligations, or liabilities. A personal lines chapter through and through.

One more definition. Twenty one zero four, subsection five, defines termination, and it does double duty. Termination means a refusal to continue to insure for reasons other than nonpayment. It includes shifting you to an affiliated company at a worse rate or with less coverage, unless you asked for the move, and offering worse renewal terms unless you asked or the old terms are gone everywhere in the state. Key insight: this chapter has no two separately numbered systems for cancellation and nonrenewal. One word, termination, one notice rule covering both. That differs from the Standard Fire Policy chapter, which splits cancellation out.

Now the heart of the domain: the duty to insure section. Twenty one one seven, not twenty one one eight, the automobile parallel, and not twenty one one nine, which only governs how underwriting rules get written and filed. Subsection one: as a condition of keeping its certificate of authority, an insurer shall not refuse to insure, refuse to continue to insure, or limit coverage available to an eligible person for home insurance, except under underwriting rules built under this section and twenty one one nine. Notice the framing: not an absolute mandate to write every applicant, but a condition on the company's license, protecting only people who qualify as an eligible person.

Subsection two is a closed list of the only bases an insurer's underwriting rules can rest on. First, the same criteria as the eligible person exclusions. Second, the physical condition of the property, but only if the rule is objective, tied to the perils insured against, and keyed to a real code or manufacturer specification, regardless of the building's age; a government compliance certificate creates a rebuttable presumption the dwelling passes. Third, for RENEWAL only, the insured's three year claim history, and only claims from the insured's own negligence or a failure, after written notice, to fix a condition tied to a paid claim.

Here is the number that shows up on almost every restoration claim: the nonrenewal claim history rule. For NONRENEWAL, an insurer can use paid claim history over the preceding three years, liability claims excluded, if there have been three or more paid claims totaling three thousand dollars or more excluding weather related claims, or three or more totaling four thousand dollars or more INCLUDING weather related claims. Three thousand excluding weather, four thousand including weather, three year window, at least three paid claims. One caution: subsection five indexes those floors to the consumer price index every sixth year from January first, two thousand six, by bulletin, so the statutory figures are the base, not necessarily today's certified numbers. A Detroit homeowner with three water damage claims in three years totaling five thousand two hundred dollars clears the four thousand dollar threshold, so a nonrenewal on that ground is lawful, if the carrier follows the notice rule.

Keep going. An insurer can nonrenew for a dwelling unoccupied more than sixty days if there is evidence of intent to vacate or keep it vacant. Forty five days with clear intent to return does not meet that bar. It can nonrenew for an adjacent physical hazard, but only if the hazard changed since the policy issued, and here is the trap: residential property or traffic patterns near the dwelling can NEVER be that hazard, however well documented. It can nonrenew when the insured failed to buy insurance in excess of eighty percent of replacement cost, but only if buying more than eighty percent was a stated sale condition and the insurer also sells a form requiring only eighty percent as its floor. And it can decline or nonrenew someone who threatened, harassed, or physically assaulted an insurer employee or agent, if reported to law enforcement.

Those rules follow a process, in twenty one one nine. Every one must be in writing, and an insurer cannot transact home insurance inconsistently with them. They must be applied uniformly and without exception statewide, so every conforming applicant is insured and every non conforming one refused, once the information is available. They get filed with DIFS for informational purposes, open to public inspection, and if DIFS finds a rule inconsistent with the chapter it can, after a hearing, order the insurer to stop using it.

Twenty one twenty one covers inspections. An insurer inspecting dwellings to decide eligibility cannot pick which properties to inspect based on race, color, creed, marital status, sex, national origin, residence, age, disability, or lawful occupation, whether it is a one time underwriting inspection or an ongoing sweep of existing business. Inspectors get civil immunity, other than contract claims, for anything related solely to physical condition findings.

Now rating factors, where a sneaky trap lives. Twenty one one one gives the closed set of factors a home rating classification can rest on: amount and type of coverage, security and safety devices, repairable structural defects tied to risk, fire protection class, construction meaning size, materials, and number of units, the insured's own controllable loss experience, use of smoking materials in the structure, distance to a fire hydrant, and availability of law enforcement or crime prevention services. Subsection nine lets an insurer use additional factors beyond that list if the plan stays consistent with the act's purposes and reflects a reasonably anticipated change in losses or expenses. Either way the plan gets filed with DIFS under twenty one zero eight, and an insurer cannot issue or renew a policy except in accordance with its filings in effect. Here's the trap: subsection four of twenty one one one bans automobile insurers from rating on sex, marital status, home ownership, education, occupation, postal zone, or credit score, but that list applies to AUTOMOBILE insurance only. Chapter twenty one has no matching prohibited list for home insurance. In fact subsection eight expressly allows home risks to be grouped by territory, so geography by itself is not banned. What IS banned is redlining, in twenty one zero eight, subsection eight: every filing must specify that the insurer will not refuse to insure, refuse to continue to insure, or limit coverage because of the location of the risk, and an insurer shall not engage in redlining.

Now the notice rule. Section twenty one twenty three, and because termination covers both cancellation and nonrenewal, this one section does the whole job. A termination is not effective unless the insurer delivers or mails written notice at least thirty days before the termination date, to the named insured's last known address, stating the effective date AND each specific reason. Shorter window for new policies: if the notice goes out within the first fifty five days after the policy was first issued, twenty days is enough. Nonpayment terminations are carved out entirely; they run on whatever schedule the policy states. And a subtle check: a termination is not effective at all unless the reason conforms to the insurer's own underwriting rules. An insurer cannot invent an off the books reason, even a true one, and have it hold up.

Before any of that, twenty one twenty two covers people who never had a policy. When an insurer or agent declines to write someone, it must give each specific reason. A written application gets a written explanation; an oral one can get an oral explanation, but the insurer must offer a written one if the applicant asks within ninety days. Refusing to even hand someone an application form counts as a declination, triggering the same duty.

What protects an insurer when it gives those reasons? Twenty one twenty four. Insurers, agents, and DIFS staff get civil immunity for statements about an insured or applicant in a cancellation, nonrenewal, or declination communication, unless made with gross negligence or in bad faith with malice in fact. That is why the blunt, factual nonrenewal letter in our example does not expose the carrier to defamation liability.

So where does a homeowner go if they think the carrier got it wrong? Section twenty one thirteen, and get this one right, because it is easy to confuse with its neighbor. It says a person who has reason to believe an insurer improperly denied them home insurance, or charged an incorrect premium, is entitled to a private informal managerial level conference with the insurer, and to review before the commissioner if that conference does not resolve the dispute. If the insurer does not provide a conference and a proposed resolution within thirty days of the request, or the person disagrees with the proposal, the person gets a determination by the commissioner, and if either side disagrees, on request the commissioner must hear it as a contested case. Its neighbor, twenty one fourteen, is limited to rate filings. Never merge the two. One caution: twenty one thirteen is written around an improper denial or an incorrect premium, and the text does not say whether a nonrenewal counts as a denial. Do not overclaim it. Alongside the statute, the everyday route is DIFS's consumer complaint process: try the insurer first, then file online or by paper form, or call DIFS at eight seven seven, nine nine nine, six four four two.

Two more pieces. Chapter twenty two, section twenty two thirty six, governs policy forms. An insurer cannot deliver a basic policy form in Michigan unless it is filed with DIFS and approved, or thirty days pass with no director action, at which point it is deemed approved. Personal lines forms must hit a readability score of at least forty five under a formula written into the statute, plus topical captions, an identified exclusions list, and a table of contents for longer forms. Use an unapproved or withdrawn form and the penalty is twenty five dollars per offense, capped at five hundred dollars per form series.

Then Chapter twenty nine, the Michigan Basic Property Insurance Association, which the statute calls the pool. This is Michigan's FAIR plan, the market of last resort, though that phrase describes how it works and is not statutory language. Membership is not optional: every insurer authorized to write the covered property and home lines, other than those writing exclusively under Chapter sixty eight, must belong as a condition of keeping its authority to transact insurance in Michigan. Its home insurance underwriting program must let every qualified applicant get home insurance for qualified property in a convenient manner, with insurance to value floors of at least eighty percent of replacement cost for a replacement cost policy, or at least one hundred percent of market value, up to one hundred twenty percent, for a repair cost policy. For basic property insurance, its premium equals the licensed rating organization's rate for identical insurance, plus a uniform, commissioner approved surcharge. And since nineteen eighty one, before every residential renewal, the pool must notify the insured of their rights to get home insurance both in the voluntary market under Chapter twenty one and through the pool under Chapter twenty nine. One trap: the pool's fraud denial disqualifier is stricter than the voluntary market's. It applies where the pool successfully denied a claim based on fraud or conspiracy to commit fraud, and it requires the denied claim to exceed two thousand dollars AND exceed fifteen percent of coverage in force for a repair cost policy, or ten percent for a replacement cost policy. Arson sits in a separate paragraph with no dollar test, and the voluntary market's arson and fraud exclusion has no dollar or percentage floor at all.

Last topic: the licensed players. Section twelve zero one, in a different chapter, defines agent as an insurance producer, and insurance producer as a person required to be licensed to sell, solicit, or negotiate insurance. It separates an agent of the insured, an unappointed producer treated as representing the insured, from an agent of the insurer, an appointed producer representing the carrier. The trap: it never defines the word adjuster. The adjuster license requirement is a separate section, twelve twenty two, subsection one: a person shall not adjust loss or damage under a policy of insurance unless licensed as an adjuster, with exactly five exemptions. Insurance counselor is a third license, section twelve thirty two: nobody can audit policies, give advice or opinion on coverage, or use words like consultant implying that license, without holding it, subject to narrow carve outs including licensed attorneys. Producer, adjuster, counselor. Three licenses, three lanes, and a restoration contractor giving coverage opinions and negotiating claim reasons for a fee sits in none.
